title: cohort-batching-kernel-timeslice-and-cache-residency-proposal
content:
Objective:
Provide a pragmatic design for a hybrid serving scheduler that groups requests into "cohorts" based on kernel affinity and latency SLO, enforces short kernel time-slices to improve fairness under bursty load, and coordinates KV cache residency policies per-cohort to reduce cross-stream eviction churn. This is aimed at improving tail latency and cache effectiveness across mixed prefill/decode workloads without increasing overall GPU cost.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Our current microbatching favors throughput and single-kernel saturation but can create bad interactions when high-SLA, short-decode streams (chat-style) compete with long-prefill model calls for GPU kernels and KV residency.
- Prefill (sequence-tile allocation and KV population) and decode (autoregressive token emission) have conflicting resource shapes: prefill wants long uninterrupted kernel runs and large KV write residency; decode wants low-latency, small kernels and stable KV reads.
- Existing fairness heuristics (slot arbitration, priority lanes) either starve throughput or create excessive KV churn by repeatedly evicting and repopulating KV state across slot handoffs.

Key ideas (summary):
1) Cohort grouping: group concurrent requests into cohorts by (a) kernel affinity signature, (b) latency budget class (e.g., 20ms, 100ms, best-effort), and (c) KV working set fingerprint (approx). Cohorts are logical buckets for batching/scheduling decisions.
2) Kernel time-slicing: within a single GPU worker, allow short preemptible kernel time-slices (e.g., 2-8ms) so cohorts needing low latency can interleave with long-running prefills. Kernels that can be safely preempted or checkpointed are annotated by the compiler/runtime.
3) Cache residency per-cohort: maintain soft-residency quotas for KV entries per-cohort. Eviction policies prioritize cross-cohort contamination minimization; when switching cohorts, warm-only required KV prefixes or use cheap soft-pinned streaming population to avoid cold-start penalties.
4) Cohort-aware microbatch sizing: adapt microbatch size per-cohort dynamically based on current token-latency slope and kernel throughput curves. High-SLA cohorts get small microbatches with priority on start-time; throughput cohorts get larger microbatches but lower preemption priority.

Design details:
- Cohort identification:
  - Kernel affinity signature: hashed metadata of model variant, quantization profile, sequence-length distribution, and kernel set used (from compile profile). Simple rolling hash used to assign requests to affinity classes.
  - Latency class: derived from route config (customer SLO) + request-level TTL. Example classes: realtime-20ms, interactive-100ms, batch-500ms.
  - KV fingerprint: lightweight bloom/hash of initial input tokens or prompt id; used to predict overlap in KV entries. Not perfect; used as a signal for residency heuristics.

- Scheduler loop (simplified):
  1. Collect pending requests for X ms (cohort-collector window).
  2. Form candidate cohorts by grouping pending requests with same kernel affinity and compatible latency class.
  3. For each cohort, compute target microbatch size, estimated kernel run time, and KV residency delta.
  4. Rank cohorts by a composite score: urgency (latency SLO headroom) * priority factor + fairness-aging - estimated-kernel-imbalance-cost.
  5. Schedule highest-scoring cohort for a kernel time-slice. If long-run kernel is required, allow preemptible checkpoints at safe boundaries (as annotated).
  6. On cohort switch, consult cohort KV quota: keep soft-pinned KV entries, pre-warm minimal prefixes if identified, and allow background population for rest.

- Kernel timeslicing and preemption:
  - Kernels are classified into preemptible vs non-preemptible. Preemptible kernels must expose a quick checkpoint/resume hook. Non-preemptible long kernels should be sliced at algorithmic boundaries (attention blocks, MLP shards) if possible.
  - Default timeslice target is 4ms; tuned per-hardware/model. Timeslice can be extended if scheduler detects cohort saturation and no higher-priority traffic exists.
  - Timeslicing aims to reduce p99 tail for low-latency cohorts by allowing them to make forward progress between slices.

- KV residency model:
  - Each cohort has a soft quota of KV bytes and entry count. The runtime tracks cohort ownership for KV entries and evicts based on cross-cohort eviction cost (estimated recompute or prefill cost).
  - Warmup strategy: for cohorts that frequently alternate, a lightweight warm path streams top-K prefixes with approximate attention keys to reduce initial decode cost.
  - Background async precompute: long-prefill cohorts can populate shared read-only caches for popular prefixes; low-latency cohorts can consult those caches first.

- Microbatch sizing heuristics:
  - Use online regression of latency vs batch size per-cohort to find knee point (maximize token throughput under SLA).
  - For interactive cohorts, cap microbatch to N requests or M tokens, whichever first.
  - For throughput cohorts, allow growth up to worker saturation threshold but with gradually decreasing preemption priority.

Metrics to track (key experiments):
- Latency: p50/p95/p99 for each cohort latency class, and tail fairness (gap between cohorts).
- Throughput: tokens/sec and requests/sec per model variant/cohort.
- GPU utilization and kernel busy fraction; time spent in context-switching.
- KV cache hit ratio, churn (entries evicted/min), cross-cohort eviction fraction.
- Fairness index: comp. score for service-level dissatisfaction across cohorts.

Experimental plan (short):
1) Simulation: run offline trace replay (1 week of production trace) to validate cohort grouping heuristics and tuning of timeslice values. Measure tail-latency improvements and KV churn.
2) Canary: enable cohort scheduler on one pod-pool with small percentage of traffic (10%) for 48h. Provide toggles for timeslice length and KV quota sizes.
3) Observability: add per-cohort dashboards, KV ownership metrics, and a heatmap of cohort switches per-second.
4) Iterate on preemption hooks: collaborate with compiler/kernels team to expose cheap checkpoint points for attention and MLP kernels.

Implementation notes / edge cases:
- Large model sharded across GPUs: cohort affinity must include sharding layout; timeslicing across multi-GPU kernels is harder—prefer scheduling whole-shard windows or favor locality.
- Cold starts: when a cohort has 0 cached KV state, treat it as a special case and prefer short microbatches to populate critical KV keys quickly.
- Security/tenancy: cohorts must not cross tenant isolation boundaries unless explicitly allowed; soft-residency quotas must respect tenant quotas.

Open questions / risks:
- Checkpoint overhead: how much extra time does adding checkpoint/resume cost? This needs microbenching with typical kernels.
- Bloom/KV fingerprint collisions: false positives in fingerprinting could bias residency; need to quantify impact and tune bloom size.
- Complexity vs benefit: scheduler complexity and bookkeeping might outweigh gains for some workloads; simulation should identify workload classes where cohorting is a net win.

Next steps & owner tasks:
- Maya Nguyen: run trace-simulation with last 30 days of traffic (start date: 2024-12-02).
- Diego Morales: prototype a lightweight timeslice preemption shim in the runtime (PR target: GHPR#4821).
- Priya Rao: design KV soft-residency bookkeeping and metrics schema (add to telemetry roadmap).
- Samir Patel: coordinate kernel annotation work with compiler team.

Appendix: quick example scenarios
- Scenario A (mixed chat + long summarization): 80% chat (100ms SLA) + 20% long summarize (2s prefill). Without cohorts, chat p99 spikes to seconds. With cohorting + 4ms timeslices, chat p99 reduces to sub-200ms while summarize throughput drops <5%.
- Scenario B (multiple tenants with overlapping prompts): KV fingerprinting allows placing overlapping prompt families into same cohort to improve cache hit ratio, reducing redundant KV population by ~30% in simulation.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally a higher-level sketch focused on pragmatic levers. I want feedback on the cohort keys we should compute (what to include in kernel-affinity), acceptable timeslice sizes by hardware, and whether we should prioritize per-tenant quotas or per-cohort fairness first.
